query: For a multi-principal element alloy system known for limited ductility in cast forms, propose a processing route and phase constitution that would simultaneously achieve nanocrystalline grain sizes below 50 nm and a dual-phase solid solution structure, thereby enhancing hardness and yield strength without inducing brittle intermetallic formation. Support this hypothesis with prior evidence regarding grain refinement mechanisms and phase stability limits, define the boundary conditions where this microstructure becomes unstable, and suggest a falsification experiment to distinguish this mechanism from simple solid solution strengthening.

generation.hypothesis: A multi-principal element alloy system with a valence electron concentration (VEC) between 4.4 and 4.6, processed via mechanical alloying followed by low-temperature spark plasma sintering (SPS) below the onset of Laves phase precipitation, will yield a nanocrystalline (<50 nm) dual-phase microstructure consisting of a disordered BCC solid solution and a nanoscale ordered B2 phase, achieving high yield strength without brittle intermetallic formation.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder mixture of refractory elements (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W, V, Ti) with a calculated atomic size difference (δ) < 6.6% and mixing enthalpy (Ω) > 1, specifically tuned to a VEC range of 4.4–4.6 to avoid brittle single-phase BCC or complex intermetallics.
generation.intervention: Mechanical alloying for 40+ hours to induce severe plastic deformation and solute mixing, followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at a temperature range (e.g., 1000–1100 °C) sufficient for consolidation but below the thermodynamic threshold for Laves phase nucleation, potentially utilizing a slight deviation from equiatomic ratios to stabilize the B2 phase.
generation.conditions: Processing atmosphere: High vacuum or inert gas (Ar); Sintering temperature: 1000–1100 °C; Holding time: < 10 minutes to suppress grain growth and phase decomposition; Cooling rate: Rapid quenching to retain the metastable nanocrystalline state.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale B2 ordered phase precipitates within the disordered BCC matrix, acting as a coherent or semi-coherent barrier to dislocation motion, while the high density of grain boundaries (nanocrystalline state) provides additional strengthening via the Hall-Petch mechanism.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism relies on the suppression of brittle intermetallic formation (like Laves phases) by maintaining the system within a specific thermodynamic window (VEC 4.4–4.6) and kinetic constraints (low SPS temperature), while leveraging the high configurational entropy to stabilize the solid solution. The dual-phase structure (B2+BCC) provides a synergistic strengthening effect where the B2 phase offers precipitation hardening and the BCC matrix ensures ductility, avoiding the brittleness associated with coarse intermetallic networks.
generation.predicted_outcome: The resulting alloy will exhibit a yield strength exceeding 1500 MPa and a fracture strain >10%, with a grain size below 50 nm and a dual-phase constitution (B2 + BCC), contrasting with the brittle behavior of single-phase BCC refractory HEAs or the coarse-grained intermetallic structures formed at higher sintering temperatures.
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory HEAs (e.g., NbMoTaW) which typically exhibit single-phase BCC structures with high strength but low room-temperature ductility, or alloys processed at high temperatures (>1200 °C) which form coarse, brittle Laves phases (e.g., Cr2Nb) as seen in PMC7866258.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis fails if the VEC exceeds 4.6, leading to brittle single-phase BCC behavior, or if the sintering temperature exceeds the critical threshold for Laves phase nucleation (observed in PMC7866258 at 1200–1400 °C), resulting in coarse intermetallics that degrade ductility. It also fails if the grain size grows beyond 50 nm due to excessive sintering time or temperature.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact thermodynamic stability window for the B2+BCC dual-phase region in non-equiatomic refractory systems, as most literature focuses on equiatomic compositions or specific systems like AlCoFeNi (PMC6197204). The kinetic stability of the nanocrystalline state during service at elevated temperatures is also uncertain, as grain growth may occur rapidly in refractory systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V-Ti alloys with VEC values of 4.5, 4.7, and 5.0. Process all via mechanical alloying and SPS at 1100 °C for 5 minutes. Compare microstructures and mechanical properties.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify phase fractions (BCC vs. B2 vs. Laves)
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to measure grain size and phase distribution
Nanoindentation and compression testing to measure yield strength and fracture strain
Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) to determine phase stability limits
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with VEC 4.5 exhibits a single-phase BCC structure with brittle fracture (strain < 5%) or if the alloy with VEC 4.5 forms coarse Laves phases (>100 nm) after SPS, the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, if the grain size exceeds 50 nm in the VEC 4.5 sample, the hypothesis regarding nanocrystalline stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution.
